# [SYNTHETIC] Structured reading logs and source evaluation in first-year composition: a randomized trial

This is a SYNTHETIC study created for a literature-review workflow example. It does not describe real participants or data.

## Methods

Students were randomly assigned by section to a structured reading log, which prompted entries on author, purpose, evidence, and corroboration, or to unstructured note-taking for one semester.

## Results

In this synthetic randomized trial of 120 first-year students, structured reading log users scored a mean of 3.4 on the five-point source evaluation rubric, compared with 2.9 for students who kept unstructured notes.

## Limitations

Rubric scoring was done by instructors who knew each student's condition, so scorer expectations may have inflated the difference.

# [SYNTHETIC] Reading logs and lateral reading behavior: a two-section quasi-experiment

This is a SYNTHETIC study created for a literature-review workflow example. It does not describe real participants or data.

## Methods

One course section used a structured reading log for all assigned research sources and the other section completed the same assignments without a log.

## Results

Across two course sections totaling 86 students, 41% of reading log users documented lateral reading of at least one source, compared with 22% of the comparison section.

## Limitations

Because sections were not randomized and had different instructors, instructor effects cannot be separated from the log intervention. Lateral reading was coded from what students wrote, so documentation and behavior are not fully distinguishable.

# [SYNTHETIC] Student perspectives on structured reading logs in research-intensive courses: an interview study

This is a SYNTHETIC study created for a literature-review workflow example. It does not describe real participants or data.

## Methods

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with students who had completed at least one course requiring a structured reading log.

## Findings

Of the 18 students interviewed, most described the reading log as useful when instructors returned written feedback on entries and as busywork when entries were ungraded.

## Limitations

Participants volunteered for interviews, so students with strong opinions about the logs may be overrepresented.

# [SYNTHETIC] Immediate and delayed effects of structured reading logs on undergraduate source evaluation: a multi-site trial

This is a SYNTHETIC study created for a literature-review workflow example. It does not describe real participants or data.

## Methods

Students in introductory research courses at three sites were randomized individually to a structured reading log or a control condition with standard assignments, and source evaluation was assessed with a blinded performance task.

## Results

Immediately after the intervention, the structured log group outperformed the control group on the source evaluation task (d = 0.31).

At the six-week delayed test, the difference between the structured log group and the control group was small and not statistically significant (d = 0.05, N = 210).

## Limitations

The delayed test used a new set of sources, so the null delayed result may reflect limited transfer rather than decay.

# Literature Review: Structured Reading Logs and Undergraduate Source Evaluation

> **SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE.** Every study cited below is a clearly synthetic, fictional fixture created to exercise the literature-review workflow. None of these studies, authors, or results exist. Do not cite or rely on any finding here as real evidence.

**Research question**: Do structured reading logs improve undergraduate students' source evaluation compared with unstructured note-taking or no log?

**Inclusion criteria**: Undergraduate learners in any discipline; an intervention built around a structured reading log with prescribed evaluative prompts; a comparison of unstructured notes, no log, or baseline; a measured source evaluation outcome or qualitative data on log use; English language. Secondary school and graduate-only populations, logs without evaluative prompts, and studies with no source evaluation outcome were excluded.

**Searches executed**: None. This workspace was built from synthetic fixtures only, so no OpenAlex, arXiv, or Europe PMC query was run and no hit counts exist. The query log in `protocol.md` records this.

## Thematic synthesis

### Framing source evaluation

Source evaluation is commonly framed as a set of judgments about authority, purpose, and corroboration that students rarely make without prompting (Ellis, 2020). Structured reading logs are one way to supply that prompting, because each entry asks the student to record the judgment explicitly.

### Immediate effects on evaluation quality

In a synthetic randomized trial of 120 first-year students, structured reading log users scored a mean of 3.4 on the five-point source evaluation rubric, compared with 2.9 for students who kept unstructured notes (Avery, 2021). A synthetic quasi-experiment across two course sections totaling 86 students found that 41% of reading log users documented lateral reading of at least one source, compared with 22% of the comparison section (Brook, 2022). Immediately after the intervention in a synthetic multi-site trial, the structured log group outperformed the control group on the source evaluation task (d = 0.31) (Dale, 2024).

Taken together, the synthetic studies agree in direction on short-term outcomes. That agreement carries limited weight, because one study used unblinded scoring and another lacked randomization.

### Durability and transfer

At the six-week delayed test, the difference between the structured log group and the control group was small and not statistically significant (d = 0.05, N = 210) (Dale, 2024). This is the only synthetic study with a delayed measure, and its delayed task used new sources, so whether gains persist remains open rather than settled.

### Implementation conditions

Of the 18 students interviewed in a synthetic study, most described the reading log as useful when instructors returned written feedback on entries and as busywork when entries were ungraded (Corvid, 2023). Feedback on log entries may therefore be a moderator worth testing directly, although no synthetic trial manipulated it.

## Certainty of evidence

The synthetic evidence points to a modest immediate benefit with uncertain durability. Consensus is not established, and the strongest design in the set shows the weakest long-term effect.

## Research gaps

- No synthetic trial varied instructor feedback on log entries, even though the interview evidence points to feedback as the condition under which students value the log.
- Only one synthetic study measured outcomes after a delay, and it used new sources, so decay and failed transfer cannot be separated.
- Behavioral outcomes such as lateral reading were coded from the logs themselves, which risks counting documentation as behavior.
- No synthetic study examined disciplines outside composition and introductory research courses.
